clue.text: The colonel finds the sea blue

blocks.note: CO is a commanding officer, which is what a colonel is to his regiment
the Baltic is the sea between Scandinavia and the rest of northern Europe

explanation.surface: An army officer gazes out at the sea and notices its colour.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: COBALTIC means containing cobalt, and blue is the colour that cobalt is famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobalt compounds give the deep pigment called cobalt blue, so a cobaltic hue is taken as that colour.

clue.text: The gunner arrived first for a snapshot

definitions.note: the clue's 'for a snapshot' names what the answer is used for, not a synonym

indicators.note: first says the word for arrived is placed ahead of the gunner

blocks.note: past tense of come
the RA is the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners

explanation.surface: An artilleryman turned up early to have his photograph taken.
explanation.walkthrough: RA, the Royal Artillery, stands for a gunner in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick photograph is taken with this device, so the clue defines it by its use.

clue.text: Deep in finance

blocks.note: first meaning: the deep is the sea, and this is a northern European sea
second meaning: the name of London's exchange for shipping freight and its financing

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are loose: 'Deep' names a sea by category, and the finance sense relies on the Baltic Exchange in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a sea, and also the short name of the City exchange where ship charters and freight are traded.

clue.text: Herb without strife is at liberty

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the word strife is taken away from the herb's name

blocks.note: a wildflower of damp ground, purple or yellow
taken as written; this is what is removed

explanation.surface: Someone called Herb, free of conflict, is now free.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb reads as a man's name, but it is the plant loosestrife.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal or prisoner that has got free is said to be on the run, unconfined.

clue.text: I get a small contribution including thanks to copy

indicators.note: including means holding within, so the thanks go inside the small contribution

blocks.note: taken as written
the widow's mite, a tiny but generous offering
ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: A small donation arrives with a thank-you, and someone wants to follow suit.
explanation.walkthrough: The widow's mite is the Gospel story of a poor woman's tiny gift; ta is everyday British for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: To reproduce or mimic something is the verb sense required here.

clue.text: Shuts the cathedral precincts

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb for fastening doors or ending business
second meaning: plural of the noun for the enclosed grounds around a cathedral

explanation.surface: Someone locks up the grounds around a cathedral at night.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface joins the two meanings into one action, but the verb and the plural noun are separate senses of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb meaning bars or seals, and a noun for walled grounds such as a cathedral's, spelt the same way.

clue.text: “There —— hugest of living creatures” (Milton)

blocks.note: surface reading: a line of verse with a word missing
setter's reading: the line from Paradise Lost book seven describing the great sea beast on the fifth day of creation

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue from Paradise Lost: 'There Leviathan, hugest of living creatures, on the deep stretched like a promontory sleeps or swims.'
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical sea monster is Milton's example of the largest animal God made, often taken as a whale.

clue.text: Old Bob finds the aircraft noisy

blocks.note: a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s
the Hawker Siddeley Trident, a British airliner of the 1960s

explanation.surface: A man called Bob finds the planes overhead loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob looks like a name; it is slang for a shilling, the pre-1971 coin whose abbreviation was s.
explanation.definitionFit: A harsh, loud and grating sound is described by this adjective.

clue.text: . . . when flying en route for Edinburgh

definitions.text: . . . when flying en route for Edinburgh

blocks.note: surface reading: continuing the previous clue, an aircraft that is noisy in flight
setter's reading: the famous express train from London King's Cross to Edinburgh, called 'Flying'

explanation.walkthrough: The dots tie this to 7 Down's aircraft, but the flying thing is a train: the Flying Scotsman.
explanation.definitionFit: Only when given the adjective 'Flying' does this word name the celebrated London to Edinburgh express locomotive and service.

clue.text: He was in yellow stockings and cross-gartered

definitions.text: He was in yellow stockings and cross-gartered

blocks.note: surface reading: a description of a man's oddly bright legwear
setter's reading: the steward in Twelfth Night tricked by a forged letter into dressing this way

explanation.walkthrough: A literary knowledge clue: in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night, the pompous steward wears yellow stockings and cross-garters to woo Olivia.
explanation.definitionFit: The forged letter tells Olivia's steward that she loves this costume, so he appears in it and is mocked.

clue.text: Finished with the party? You have to exaggerate

blocks.note: something finished is over
a do is an informal word for a party; 'with' joins it on

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether you're done celebrating and accuses you of laying it on too thick.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English a 'do' is a party or social function.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry something too far or make too much of it is a common sense of the verb.

clue.text: Opposite directions to a horse can be a drawback

blocks.note: south, read with the north that the horse word begins with
a nag is an old or worn-out horse

explanation.surface: Pulling a horse two ways at once causes trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The parse is loose: 'Opposite directions' suggests S and N, but only S is added, the N coming from the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden obstacle or unexpected problem is a common noun sense of the answer.

clue.text: Cause a disturbance like Adam and Eve

blocks.note: first meaning: an idiom for making an angry fuss
second meaning: read literally, what the first parents did in bringing up their elder son

explanation.surface: Someone stirs up trouble, behaving as the first couple did in Eden.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, Adam and Eve's first son is Cain, so the idiom is also literally true of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to make a great commotion; taken literally it describes parents rearing their son Cain.

clue.text: Mountains held in grand esteem

indicators.note: something held in is enclosed by the words that follow, so look inside them

blocks.note: the run of letters across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Some mountains are greatly respected.
explanation.definitionFit: The range running down the western side of South America is the longest continental mountain chain.

clue.text: Dwelling place of one worried by population explosion

definitions.text: Dwelling place of one worried by population explosion

blocks.clueFragment: Dwelling place of one worried by population explosion
blocks.note: surface reading: the home of someone anxious about overcrowding on the planet
setter's reading: the old woman of the nursery rhyme, who had so many children she didn't know what to do

explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme begins 'There was an old woman who lived in a shoe'; her 'population explosion' is her huge family.
explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme, an item of footwear serves as the crowded house of the overwhelmed mother.

clue.text: The mistress gives you the needle

blocks.note: first meaning: the woman who runs a household
second meaning: a small sewing case holding needles and thread, pronounced 'hussif'

explanation.surface: The lady of the house irritates you.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives you the needle' sounds like annoying someone, but the second sense is the old name for a pocket sewing kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman managing a home, and a soldier's or traveller's compact kit of needles and thread, share one word.

clue.text: It's just hell here

blocks.note: surface reading: a casual complaint that a place is unbearable
setter's reading: the place literally is hell, the biblical valley whose name became a word for it

explanation.walkthrough: The complaint is taken literally. The answer is a Hebrew place name, the valley outside Jerusalem that came to stand for hell.
explanation.definitionFit: In Jewish and Christian scripture the name of that cursed valley is used as a word for the place of damnation.

clue.text: Pickpockets have little time to measure the depth

definitions.note: the clue gives the purpose; the answer is a noun for the tool

blocks.note: a dip is slang for a pickpocket
a tick is a moment, as in 'just a tick'

explanation.surface: Thieves have only a moment to gauge how deep something is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just a tick' is British for 'just a moment'.
explanation.definitionFit: The graduated rod pushed into an engine's oil sump or a tank is used for checking the level of liquid.

clue.text: The censor or the rain can do it

blocks.note: first meaning: the official who could ban a stage production
second meaning: what a downpour does to a cricket match

explanation.walkthrough: Until 1968 the Lord Chamberlain censored British plays; 'rain stopped play' is the familiar cricket report.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre censor could halt a drama, and weather halting a game is reported with exactly this phrase.

clue.text: Friends like to keep it out of play

blocks.note: first meaning: the phrase friends use about staying in contact, 'keep ...'
second meaning: in football and rugby, the ball is out of play when it crosses the side line

explanation.surface: Pals prefer to stay out of the game.
explanation.walkthrough: The touchline is the side boundary of a football or rugby pitch; a ball beyond it is said to be in touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Friends maintain contact by keeping in touch, and a ball over the sideline is also described with the same phrase.

clue.text: Pledge with wine?

blocks.note: first meaning: to pawn something, as in 'in ...'
second meaning: a German white wine from the Rhine

explanation.surface: A toast raised with a glass of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pledge with wine' suggests drinking a toast. Hock is the British name for Rhine wine.
explanation.definitionFit: To pawn an item is an informal verb sense, and white Rhenish wine is the noun sense.

clue.text: Dishonest inclination

blocks.note: first meaning: slang adjective for corrupt
second meaning: a natural tendency or talent

explanation.surface: A crooked tendency.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is slang for crooked, and as a noun it means a natural aptitude or leaning.

clue.text: Confused with one of nine in bed

indicators.note: in places one item inside the other, so the nine-sister figure lies within the bed

blocks.note: taken as written
the Muses were the nine Greek goddesses of the arts

explanation.surface: Someone bewildered at finding one of a group of nine lying in bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Puzzled and bewildered are synonyms of this past participle, meaning thoroughly perplexed.

clue.text: Paper with an after-tea edition

indicators.note: after says the edition is set down following the tea

blocks.note: tea sounds like the letter T
an issue is one edition of a publication

explanation.surface: A newspaper with a late-afternoon edition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a newspaper; the answer is thin paper. Tea standing for the letter T is a common crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin, soft paper used for wrapping or for blowing the nose is called by this name.

clue.text: A fellow's representatives

blocks.note: taken as written
a gent is a fellow, a gentleman; the apostrophe is ignored

explanation.surface: The people who act on behalf of some man.
explanation.definitionFit: People acting on behalf of others, such as business or literary representatives, are this plural noun.

clue.text: The composer to give us pep

indicators.note: letters that give are made to yield and bend, so the words after are rearranged

blocks.note: these five letters are the material to rearrange

explanation.surface: A request that some composer's music liven us up.
explanation.walkthrough: Franz von Suppé was the Austrian composer of the Light Cavalry and Poet and Peasant overtures.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the surname of a nineteenth-century Viennese writer of operettas and lively overtures.

clue.text: Striving with the favourite in the future

indicators.note: one thing set in another sits inside it, so the favourite goes within the word for the future

blocks.note: the coming days are the future; 'coming' means forthcoming
a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: A contender trying hard, backed by the favourite to win later.
explanation.walkthrough: The future word splits after its first three letters to take the favourite inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To be vying or contending with rivals is to strive against them.

clue.text: It is not eleven-plus for the continental pupil

indicators.note: not denies that the word is complete, so the number loses its closing letter

blocks.note: the number taken from the exam's name

explanation.surface: A foreign schoolchild does not sit the eleven-plus exam.
explanation.walkthrough: The eleven-plus was the English exam at age eleven for grammar school places. ELEVE plus N would make ELEVEN, so it 'is not eleven'.
explanation.definitionFit: In French the everyday word for a schoolchild or student, so 'continental' signals a foreign-language word.

clue.text: Is thick — with patines of bright gold" (M.O.V.)

definitions.text: Is thick — with patines of bright gold" (M.O.V.)

blocks.clueFragment: Is thick — with patines of bright gold
blocks.note: surface reading: a line of Shakespeare with a word missing
setter's reading: Lorenzo's speech under the stars in The Merchant of Venice, act five

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: 'Look how the floor of heaven is thick ... with patines of bright gold'. M.O.V. is The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: The stars are pictured as small golden plates set into the sky like decoration worked into a surface.

clue.text: Introduces America to her offence

blocks.note: US is the abbreviation for the United States
taken as written
a sin is a moral offence

explanation.surface: Someone tells America about a wrong she has done.
explanation.definitionFit: To show someone into a room, or bring something in for the first time, is a phrasal verb meaning presents.

clue.text: Indispensable chaps to let you in

definitions.text: Indispensable chaps to let you in

blocks.note: surface reading: the essential people in an organisation
setter's reading: men who hold the keys that open the doors

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for vital staff is read literally, as men carrying keys who can unlock a building for you.
explanation.definitionFit: Essential employees are described as crucial personnel, and the literal sense is doorkeepers holding the means of opening locks.

clue.text: You must get love in it for heartsease

definitions.text: You must get love in it for heartsease

blocks.clueFragment: You must get love in it
blocks.note: surface reading: advice that affection will bring peace of mind
setter's reading: put the words 'love in' before the answer to get another name of the flower heartsease

explanation.walkthrough: Heartsease, the wild pansy, is also called love-in-idleness, the flower whose juice works the love spell in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Prefixed by the words 'love in', this noun for laziness completes an old country name for the wild pansy.
